title: Trace a Building's Gravity Load Path
prompt: Walk me through how gravity load travels from a typical office floor down to the foundation. Take a representative interior bay, assign realistic dead and live loads, and trace the load through the slab, beams, girders, columns, and footing. Size one representative simply-supported beam as you go, and tell me how you'd think about the lateral system too.
blurb: Spoken station — trace gravity load from slab to foundation: tributary areas, dead/live loads, load combinations, a worked beam sizing, and lateral-system awareness.

rubric.label: Load path & tributary areas
rubric.description: Traces gravity load in the correct sequence — slab spans to beams, beams to girders, girders to columns, columns to foundation — and defines tributary width/area at each step so that load is neither lost nor double-counted.

rubric.label: Load quantification
rubric.description: Assigns realistic dead and live loads (e.g., office live ~50 psf, slab/superimposed dead loads), distinguishes dead vs live vs superimposed, and converts area loads to line loads on members using tributary width.

rubric.label: Load combinations
rubric.description: Applies factored (LRFD/strength) combinations such as 1.2D + 1.6L and mentions service-level combos for deflection; understands why factors differ and which combo typically governs gravity design.

rubric.label: Member sizing & calculation
rubric.description: Sizes a simply-supported beam correctly — max moment wL^2/8, required section modulus S = M/Fb (or Mu/(phi*Fy)), and a deflection/serviceability sanity check — with a clean worked numeric example.

rubric.label: Lateral-system awareness
rubric.description: Recognizes that gravity is only part of the story; identifies a lateral force-resisting system (moment frames, braced frames, shear walls) and how lateral load and its own load path coexist with gravity.

rubric.label: Assumptions & sanity checks
rubric.description: States assumptions (support conditions, continuity, spans), checks units, and applies rules of thumb (e.g., span/depth ratios) to sanity-check results.

rubric.label: Communication & structure
rubric.description: Explains the reasoning in an organized, sequential way; thinks aloud; keeps track of load bookkeeping from floor to footing.

reference.scenario: The candidate is asked to trace the gravity load path for a typical multistory office building and to size a representative member along the way. The station tests whether they understand that load accumulates through a hierarchy of members — slab to beam to girder to column to foundation — and can quantify it with realistic loads, apply strength load combinations, and perform a clean beam-sizing calculation with a serviceability check. The interviewer can vary the bay size, span, or occupancy to see whether the candidate's numbers update correctly. This is an educational reasoning exercise, not a substitute for a licensed engineer's design, code-checked calculations, or project-specific sign-off.
model_points: States the gravity load hierarchy explicitly: floor slab spans to floor beams, beams frame into girders, girders deliver load to columns, columns stack load downward and deliver it to spread/mat/pile foundations that spread it to the soil.

Uses tributary area/width to apportion load: each beam picks up a strip equal to half the distance to the adjacent members on each side; a column's tributary area is roughly the bay area it supports (e.g., a 30 ft x 30 ft interior bay gives ~900 sq ft per floor).

Assigns realistic loads: office live load ~50 psf (plus ~20 psf partition allowance), superimposed dead ~15-25 psf (MEP, ceiling, flooring), and slab self-weight (e.g., a 6 in normal-weight concrete slab ~75 psf); names ASCE 7 as the load source.
Applies LRFD strength load combinations, principally 1.2D + 1.6L, and mentions others (e.g., 1.4D, and combinations with wind/seismic); uses unfactored service loads for deflection checks.
Converts area load to a line load on a beam: w = (factored area load) x (tributary width); e.g., a beam at 10 ft spacing under ~150 psf factored carries ~1.5 kip/ft.
Computes design forces for a simply-supported beam: maximum moment M = wL^2/8 and maximum shear V = wL/2 at midspan/supports respectively.
Sizes the beam by strength: required section modulus S >= M/Fb (ASD) or required Zx from Mu = phi*Fy*Zx (LRFD, phi = 0.90), then selects a rolled shape (e.g., a W-shape) meeting or exceeding it.

Checks serviceability: live-load deflection limit around L/360 (and L/240 total), using delta = 5wL^4/(384EI) for a uniformly loaded simple span, and applies span/depth rules of thumb (steel beam depth ~ L/20 to L/24).
Accumulates axial load in columns floor by floor (tributary area x load per floor x number of floors, with live-load reduction on large tributary areas) and sizes the footing from that total.

Distinguishes the gravity system from the lateral force-resisting system (moment frames, braced frames, shear walls, diaphragms) and notes lateral load has its own path (diaphragm to vertical elements to foundation) that must coexist with gravity.

probes.trigger: candidate leaves load in the slab and jumps to columns
probes.question: Before it reaches the column, what member does the slab load pass through, and how do you decide how much each beam picks up?

probes.trigger: candidate uses an area load directly on a beam
probes.question: Your load is in psf but the beam is a line member — how do you get from pounds per square foot to a load per foot along the beam?
Are you designing the strength of this beam to service loads or factored loads? What combination would you apply and why?

probes.trigger: candidate forgets the maximum-moment formula or misplaces it
probes.question: For a uniformly loaded simply-supported beam, where is the maximum moment and what's its magnitude?

probes.trigger: candidate sizes for strength only and stops
probes.question: The beam is strong enough — but would the occupants notice anything? What else governs the section?
You've handled gravity. What resists wind or seismic load on this building, and how does that load reach the foundation?

red_flags: Losing or double-counting load — e.g., not using tributary width, or adding girder load without the beams that feed it.
Applying an area load (psf) directly to a line member without converting to load per foot.
Designing member strength to unfactored service loads instead of factored combinations.
Misstating the simple-span moment (using wL^2/2 or wL/8 instead of wL^2/8).
Ignoring deflection/serviceability and sizing on strength alone.
Grossly unrealistic loads (e.g., 5 psf or 500 psf office live load) with no sanity check.
Confusing the gravity load path with the lateral system, or claiming gravity framing alone resists wind and seismic.
Unit errors — mixing psf, plf, kips, and inches without tracking them.
follow_ups: How does live-load reduction change the column and footing loads on a large tributary area over many floors?
If this beam were continuous over several supports instead of simply supported, how would the moment diagram and your governing moment change?
How would a composite steel-concrete floor change the beam's effective stiffness and your deflection check?
Trace the lateral load path for a wind event: from the facade to the diaphragm to the vertical system to the foundation.
How do you size the spread footing once you know the total service axial load at the base of the column?
reference.exemplar_answer: I'd start at the top and follow the load down. The floor slab spans between floor beams and delivers a distributed pressure to them; each beam picks up a tributary strip equal to half the spacing to the beams on either side, so a beam at 10 ft spacing collects a 10 ft-wide strip. Those beams frame into girders, the girders land on columns, the columns stack the accumulated load floor by floor, and the bottom column delivers everything to a footing that spreads it into the soil. For loads on a typical office floor I'd take a 6-inch normal-weight slab at about 75 psf, superimposed dead of roughly 20 psf for ceiling, MEP and flooring, and an office live load of 50 psf plus a partition allowance — call dead about 95 psf and live about 65 psf. For strength I design to factored load, 1.2D + 1.6L, which is about 1.2(95) + 1.6(65) is roughly 218 psf; on a beam at 10 ft tributary width that's about 2.2 kip/ft. Say the beam simply spans 30 ft: the maximum moment is wL^2/8 = 2.2 x 30^2 / 8 is about 248 kip-ft, and the shear is wL/2 is about 33 kips. Sizing in steel with Fy = 50 ksi, LRFD needs Zx >= Mu/(phi*Fy) = 248 x 12 / (0.9 x 50) is about 66 in^3, so I'd pick a W-shape with Zx a bit above that, maybe a W18x40-ish section, then confirm the depth is sensible against the L/20-to-L/24 rule and check live-load deflection against L/360 using 5wL^4/384EI on service load. Columns then accumulate tributary bay load times the number of floors, with live-load reduction on the large tributary, and that total sizes the footing. All of that is the gravity path; separately, wind or seismic load goes from the cladding into the floor diaphragms and then into a lateral system — moment frames, braced frames, or shear walls — which carries it down to the foundation, so the building really has two load paths working at once.

interviewer_notes: Mid-level structural station. Let the candidate establish the load hierarchy first, then feed specifics — a bay size, a span, an occupancy — to see whether their numbers update correctly and stay dimensionally consistent. The single most important behavior is clean load bookkeeping: load must flow slab to beam to girder to column to footing via tributary areas without being lost or double-counted, and area loads (psf) must be converted to line loads (plf) before member design. Reward a correct wL^2/8 moment, a strength check to factored combinations (1.2D + 1.6L), and a serviceability/deflection check, plus awareness that gravity and lateral systems are distinct. Do not require exact code-book values, rolled-shape properties from memory, or licensed-engineer precision — reward correct method, realistic estimates, and sanity checks. This is a reasoning exercise, not a code compliance calculation.
